cards.back: CK, LDH, AST/ALT, aldolase • MRI T2/STIR muscle oedema • biopsy: perifascicular atrophy • Rx: steroids + methotrexate; IVIG if severe.

cards.front: Summarise scleroderma in children.
cards.back: Commonest: localised (linear) → methotrexate ± steroids, physiotherapy. Systemic sclerosis rare: anti-Scl-70 (diffuse, ILD), anticentromere (limited). CCB for Raynaud, ACE inhibitor for renal crisis.

III-10.summary: HSP (IgA vasculitis) is the commonest childhood vasculitis: palpable purpura on buttocks and legs with a normal platelet count, plus joints, gut and kidneys. Treatment is supportive; steroids ease severe gut pain but do not prevent nephritis — so check urine and BP for 6-12 months.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy, 10 days after a sore throat, develops a raised purpuric rash over the buttocks and the backs of his legs, swollen painful ankles and colicky abdominal pain. He is afebrile and well perfused; platelet count and clotting are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Palpable purpura in a gravity-dependent distribution with a normal platelet count, arthritis and abdominal pain after an URTI = HSP. ITP and ALL have low platelets; meningococcal sepsis gives a febrile, unwell child with non-palpable spreading purpura.
questions.note: Palpable purpura on buttocks and legs (always).

questions.stem: Three days into an episode of HSP, a 5-year-old develops sudden severe paroxysmal abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs and passes redcurrant-jelly stool. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explain: Bowel-wall oedema and haemorrhage in HSP act as a lead point for intussusception, typically ileo-ileal (unlike idiopathic ileocolic) — so ultrasound is needed and air enema may not reduce it.
questions.note: Gut → colic, bleeding, ileo-ileal intussusception; kidney → haematuria, proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has a classical clinical picture of HSP with purpura and arthritis. Which investigations are essential at diagnosis and at follow-up?
options: ANCA, ANA and anti-dsDNA serology in all children
Urine protein-creatinine ratio and blood pressure
questions.explain: HSP is a clinical diagnosis; what matters is detecting nephritis — urinalysis/uPCR and blood pressure (with FBC and clotting normal). Skin or renal biopsy is reserved for atypical cases or significant renal involvement.
questions.note: FBC/clotting normal; urine protein-creatinine ratio, BP; US if severe pain.

questions.stem: The parents of a 6-year-old with HSP and mild abdominal pain ask whether giving prednisolone now will stop him developing kidney disease. What is the correct answer?
options: No; they ease severe gut pain only
questions.explain: Trials show corticosteroids relieve severe abdominal (and joint) pain but do not prevent HSP nephritis, so they are not given prophylactically; urine and BP monitoring is what protects the kidney.
questions.note: Steroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with HSP has normal urinalysis and blood pressure at presentation and the rash is fading. What follow-up is most appropriate?
options: No follow-up needed if urine is normal now
A single repeat urinalysis at 1 week
Urine and BP checks for 4 weeks only
Urine and BP monitoring for 6-12 months
questions.explain: Nephritis (20-50%) usually appears within 4-6 weeks but can occur later, and it determines long-term prognosis; urine dipstick and BP should be monitored for 6-12 months even if initially normal.
questions.note: Monitor urine and blood pressure for 6-12 months.

questions.stem: Which pairing of childhood vasculitis with predominant vessel size is correct?
questions.explain: Takayasu arteritis affects the aorta and its branches (large), Kawasaki disease the coronary arteries (medium), and HSP/IgA vasculitis capillaries and venules (small).
questions.note: Takayasu is large-vessel, Kawasaki medium-vessel; granulomatosis with polyangiitis: c-ANCA (PR3).

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with HSP has painful swollen knees, microscopic haematuria and a raised urine protein-creatinine ratio. Which analgesic is most appropriate?
questions.explain: With renal involvement, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) should be avoided because they can worsen kidney function; paracetamol is preferred. Steroids are not first-line analgesia for arthritis.
questions.note: Supportive: rest, paracetamol (acetaminophen), fluids; NSAIDs only if kidneys normal.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old has chronic bloody nasal discharge, recurrent sinusitis, haemoptysis with cavitating lung nodules and haematuria with red cell casts. Serology shows c-ANCA with anti-PR3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Upper airway + cavitating lung + renal disease with c-ANCA/PR3 = granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Microscopic polyangiitis is p-ANCA (MPO) without granulomatous ENT disease; anti-GBM has no ENT involvement or ANCA.
questions.note: Takayasu is large-vessel, Kawasaki medium-vessel; granulomatosis with polyangiitis: c-ANCA (PR3).

cards.front: Describe the clinical picture of Henoch-Schönlein purpura.
cards.back: Commonest childhood vasculitis, 3-10 y, after URTI, autumn/winter • palpable purpura buttocks/legs (always), normal platelets • arthritis ankles/knees ~75% • colicky pain ~50-75% (ileo-ileal intussusception) • nephritis 20-50% within 4-6 weeks.

cards.front: How do you diagnose and manage HSP?
cards.back: Clinical: purpura (mandatory) + abdominal pain, IgA histology, arthritis or renal involvement • FBC/clotting normal; uPCR, BP; US if severe pain • supportive: paracetamol, fluids; NSAIDs only if kidneys normal; steroids for severe gut pain (don't prevent nephritis) • urine + BP 6-12 months.

cards.front: Classify childhood vasculitides by vessel size.
cards.back: Large: Takayasu • medium: Kawasaki (polyarteritis nodosa) • small: HSP/IgA vasculitis, ANCA vasculitis — granulomatosis with polyangiitis = c-ANCA (PR3).
